questions.title: Which drug is first-line for essential tremor?
questions.question: An elderly patient with benign prostatic hyperplasia is found to have a fine, bilateral action tremor of the hands, diagnosed as essential tremor. Which drug is first-line pharmacological treatment?

explanations.A: Correct. Propranolol, a non-selective beta-adrenergic antagonist, is first-line pharmacological therapy for essential tremor: blocking peripheral beta-2 receptors in skeletal muscle reduces tremor amplitude, and it is used across age groups including elderly patients (with appropriate caution for comorbidities). Recognising this first-line choice is clinically important, since essential tremor is often mistaken for the resting tremor of Parkinson disease, which responds to different drugs.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Levodopa is the mainstay treatment for the resting tremor of Parkinson disease, not the action/postural tremor of essential tremor, and is not first-line here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Amantadine is an antiparkinsonian agent, not a first-line treatment for essential tremor.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Diazepam is not a first-line pharmacological treatment for essential tremor; propranolol is preferred.

questions.learning_objective: State that propranolol is used to treat essential tremor.

questions.title: What is the classic presentation of anterior spinal artery occlusion at the spinal cord level?
questions.question: Occlusion of the anterior spinal artery at the level of the spinal cord classically produces which pattern of deficit below the lesion?

options.A: Bilateral flaccid paraplegia with bilateral loss of pain and temperature, dorsal columns spared
options.B: Ipsilateral tongue weakness with contralateral limb weakness
options.C: Ipsilateral loss of proprioception with contralateral loss of pain and temperature
options.D: Complete bilateral sensory and motor loss including proprioception

explanations.A: Correct. The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord; its occlusion at the spinal cord level causes bilateral paraplegia below the lesion with bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation, while the dorsal columns (proprioception, vibration), supplied by the posterior spinal arteries, are classically spared. Recognising this pattern clinically distinguishes a spinal cord-level vascular syndrome from the different combination of deficits seen with a brainstem-level anterior spinal artery territory lesion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ipsilateral tongue weakness with contralateral limb weakness describes medial medullary syndrome, from anterior spinal artery territory occlusion at the medulla, a different level with a different, more localised picture.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This pattern describes Brown-Sequard syndrome (spinal cord hemisection), not bilateral anterior spinal artery occlusion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Anterior spinal artery occlusion classically spares the dorsal columns (posterior spinal artery territory), so proprioception is not lost.

questions.learning_objective: State that anterior spinal artery occlusion at the spinal cord level causes bilateral paraplegia with bilateral loss of pain and temperature, sparing the dorsal columns.

questions.title: Which drug reverses fentanyl intoxication?
questions.question: A patient presents with respiratory depression and pinpoint pupils after suspected fentanyl overdose. Which drug is given to acutely reverse the intoxication?

explanations.A: Correct. Naloxone, a short-acting competitive mu-opioid receptor antagonist, is given intravenously or intramuscularly to acutely reverse opioid (including fentanyl) intoxication, restoring respiratory drive and consciousness within minutes; repeated dosing may be needed since fentanyl can outlast naloxone's effect. Because fentanyl is a potent, long-acting opioid, patients reversed with naloxone must be monitored closely for re-sedation as the antagonist wears off before the opioid does.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Naltrexone is a long-acting oral opioid antagonist used for relapse prevention after detoxification, not for acute overdose reversal.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine receptor antagonist, used to reverse benzodiazepine (not opioid) overdose.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Buprenorphine is a partial mu-opioid agonist used in analgesia and substitution therapy; it is not the acute reversal agent for opioid overdose and could itself precipitate withdrawal if given during acute intoxication.

questions.learning_objective: State that naloxone is used to acutely reverse fentanyl (opioid) intoxication.

questions.title: Which nucleus is the origin of the trapezoid body?
questions.question: The trapezoid body, a bundle of decussating auditory fibres in the ventral pons, arises from which nucleus?

explanations.A: Correct. The trapezoid body arises from the (ventral) cochlear nucleus, the first central relay for auditory information; many of its fibres cross the midline within the trapezoid body to reach the contralateral superior olivary nucleus. This crossing at the trapezoid body is what gives the central auditory pathway its bilateral, partially crossed representation needed for sound localisation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The superior olivary nucleus is a destination the trapezoid body's fibres synapse upon after crossing, not its nucleus of origin.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The inferior colliculus is further along the auditory pathway, receiving input after the superior olivary complex, not the origin of the trapezoid body.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The medial geniculate body is the thalamic auditory relay, much further along the pathway, not the origin of the trapezoid body.

questions.learning_objective: State that the cochlear nucleus is the origin of the trapezoid body.
